sections.html: This interesting driftwood catfish is only rarely available and in small numbers. It reaches a maximum length of about 14-15 cm. Two features are very obvious: the large eyes and the large pectoral fins, which are always spread.
Jeremy Basch of AmazonTropics.com, an expert on these catfishes, states that unfortunately this species is not really a good aquarium candidate because of its constant swimming.
The species is widely distributed in the Amazon and Orinoco river basins. The specimens described here originate from Peru, which is also the type locality of the species.
South America: Amazon and Orinoco River basins. Type locality: Marañon River, upper Amazon and Napo Rivers.
One might see better results in a tank with a constant stream of water that goes across the tank. This would require a fairly large pump or many jet lifters.

In its native habitat they feed on small invertebrates and crustaceans. In the aquarium they will eat anything given, such as frozen bloodworm, catfish tablets, white worm (sparingly), prawns and shrimp.

This species constantly swims in the aquarium and seems to be unable to detect the sides of the tank. It never goes and hides; they literally swim 99% of the time. They are only occasionally seen resting on the ground, which is uncommon.
The sexes can be distinguished best by the shape of the maxillary barbels: these barbels are curved in males and straight in females.
The sexes can be distinguished best by the shape of the maxillary barbels: these barbels are curved in males and straight in females.
The spines of the pectoral fins should be handled with care: one can be stung nastily by them, and the spines also tend to tangle in the mesh of a net when the fish has to be caught.

Mees (1974) assigned this species to Tatia but Ferraris (2007) reverted it to the original genus Centromochlus.

Etymology: The genus name Centromochlus: kentron, thorn or spine; mochlus, lever or crowbar, presumably referring to the strongly serrated dorsal-fin spine. The specific name heckelii: in honour of Johann Jakob Heckel (1790-1857), curator of fishes, Naturhistorisches Museum in Vienna.

Two features of the fish are very obvious: the large eyes and the large pectoral fins, which are always spread. The pectoral-fin spines should be handled with care as one can be stung by them, and the spines also tend to tangle in the mesh of a net when the fish needs to be caught.

IUCN Red List: despite there being little information available on this species, it is assessed as Least Concern due to its wide range and no direct threat (IUCN 2023).
